# react-socket — Full Reference

> TypeScript-first WebSocket library for React. Published on npm as `@luciodale/react-socket`.
> Docs: https://koolcodez.com/projects/react-socket
> npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@luciodale/react-socket
> Source: https://github.com/luciodale/react-socket
> License: MIT. Author: Lucio D'Alessandro.

## What it is

react-socket is a WebSocket manager for React apps. You declare your client and
server message types as discriminated unions, create one `WebSocketManager` at
module level, and consume it through twelve single-purpose hooks. The library
owns the parts people usually rewrite by hand: reconnection with exponential
backoff and jitter, ref-counted subscriptions that dedupe across components and
restore after a drop, ack/in-flight tracking, ping/pong keep-alive, and an
optional offline send queue.

It speaks plain WebSocket. No custom wire protocol, no server SDK — any backend
that serves a WebSocket endpoint works (Node, Go, Rust, Cloudflare Durable
Objects, Elixir, Python).

## Install

```bash
npm install @luciodale/react-socket
# pnpm add @luciodale/react-socket
# yarn add @luciodale/react-socket
# bun add @luciodale/react-socket
```

Requirements: React 18+ (hooks are built on `useSyncExternalStore`),
TypeScript 4.7+ recommended, modern evergreen browsers. Zero runtime
dependencies.

Entry points:
- `@luciodale/react-socket` — manager + hooks
- `@luciodale/react-socket/inspector` — devtools panel (tree-shakes out of prod)
- `@luciodale/react-socket/testing` — fake transport for unit tests

## Quick start

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react"
import {
  WebSocketManager,
  useSocketEvent,
  useSocketSend,
} from "@luciodale/react-socket"

type TClientMsg = { type: "echo"; text: string }
type TServerMsg = { type: "echo"; text: string }

const manager = new WebSocketManager<TClientMsg, TServerMsg>({
  url: "wss://your-server.com/ws",
  serialize: (msg) => JSON.stringify(msg),
  deserialize: (raw) => JSON.parse(raw),
})

export function Echo() {
  const [response, setResponse] = useState<string | null>(null)
  const { send } = useSocketSend(manager)

  useSocketEvent(manager, "echo", (msg) => setResponse(msg.text))

  useEffect(() => {
    manager.connect()
    return () => manager.disconnect()
  }, [])

  return (
    <button onClick={() => send({ type: "echo", text: "hello" })}>send</button>
  )
}
```

## The twelve hooks

- `useSocketEvent(manager, type, cb)` — react to one incoming message type; the
  callback argument is narrowed via `Extract<TServerMsg, { type: T }>`.
- `useSocketEventBatch(manager, type, cb, { flushMs })` — same, but buffers and
  flushes on an interval. For high-frequency streams (ticks, telemetry).
- `useSocketSubscription(manager, { key, subscribe, unsubscribe })` — ref-counted
  server-side subscription. N components with the same key produce one subscribe
  message; the unsubscribe fires when the last one unmounts.
- `useSocketPendingSubscription(manager, key)` — `true` while a subscribe is in
  flight; drives "joining…" UI.
- `useSocketSend(manager)` — returns `{ send }`. `send(data, ackId?)` returns a
  boolean indicating whether the message left the client.
- `useSocketSendIntent(manager, cb)` — fires on every `send()`, even offline.
  This is the optimistic-update hook.
- `useSocketSendFailed(manager, cb)` — fires when a send never left the client;
  `reason` is `"not-connected" | "serialize-error" | "transport-error"`.
- `useSocketInFlightDrop(manager, cb)` — fires with the messages dropped when a
  connection closes before their acks arrived.
- `useSocketReady(manager, cb)` — fires after every (re)connect with the list of
  restored subscription keys.
- `useSocketLastUnsubscribe(manager, cb)` — fires when the last subscriber for a
  key unmounts; second argument is the original subscribe payload.
- `useSocketConnectionState(manager)` — re-rendering connection state.
- `useSocketConnectionChange(manager, cb)` — event counterpart, no re-render.

Connection states: `"idle" | "disconnected" | "connecting" | "connected" | "reconnecting"`.
`"idle"` means `connect()` was never called — distinct from `"disconnected"`.

## Manager configuration (`TManagerConfig`)

Required:
- `url: string | (() => string | Promise<string>)` — static or resolved per attempt.
- `serialize: (msg: TClientMsg) => TWire`
- `deserialize: (raw: TIncoming) => TServerMsg`

Optional:
- `discriminator` — key used to narrow server messages. Defaults to `"type"`.
- `transport` — inject a custom `IWebSocketTransport` (used by the testing entry point).
- `binaryType` — `"blob" | "arraybuffer"` for binary frames.
- `pingIntervalMs`, `pongTimeoutMs`, `ping()`, `isPong(msg)` — keep-alive.
- `pauseHeartbeatWhenHidden` — defaults to `true`; avoids spurious pong timeouts
  from background-tab throttling.
- `reconnectMaxAttempts` (default 10), `reconnectBaseDelayMs`, `reconnectMaxDelayMs`.
- `getAckId(msg)` — return the ack id carried by a server message; the library
  clears the matching in-flight entry automatically.
- `getSubscriptionResolvedKey(msg)` — return the subscription key a server
  message confirms; clears the pending-subscription flag.
- `beforeConnect({ trigger, attempt })` — awaited before every attempt (first
  connect, each retry, `forceReconnect()`), and before a dynamic `url()`
  resolves. The place to refresh an auth token. If it throws, the attempt aborts
  to `"disconnected"` with no auto-retry.
- `onReady(restoredKeys)` — fires after the socket opens. Use for first-message auth.
- `onDebug(event)` — every lifecycle event; powers the Inspector.

## Manager methods

`connect()`, `disconnect()`, `forceReconnect()`, `dispose()`, `send({ data, ackId })`,
`subscribe(key, data?)`, `unsubscribe(key, data?)`, `getRefCount(key)`,
`hasPendingSubscription(key)`, `ackInFlight(ackId)`, `resolvePendingSubscription(key)`,
`getConnectionState()`, `getSnapshot()`, `setProtocols(protocols)`, plus
`addXxxListener` methods mirroring each hook for non-React call sites.

## Acknowledged sends

```ts
const manager = new WebSocketManager<TClientMsg, TServerMsg>({
  url: "wss://...",
  serialize: JSON.stringify,
  deserialize: (raw) => JSON.parse(raw),
  getAckId: (msg) => (msg.type === "delivered" ? msg.ackId : undefined),
})

const id = crypto.randomUUID()
send({ type: "message", id, text }, id) // second arg is the ack id
```

## Subscriptions

```tsx
useSocketSubscription(manager, {
  key: roomId,
  subscribe: { type: "subscribe", channel: roomId },
  unsubscribe: (sub) => ({ type: "unsubscribe", channel: sub.channel }),
})
```

Three components mounting the same `roomId` send one subscribe message. When all
three unmount, one unsubscribe fires. Reconnect replays the subscription.

## Authentication

Two shapes, both first-class:
- Token in the connection: `url: () => \`wss://host/ws?token=\${auth.token}\`` plus
  `beforeConnect` to refresh it before each attempt.
- Token as the first message: send it from `onReady`, which fires after open.

## Offline queue (undelivered sync)

`createUndeliveredSync` keeps per-channel lists of messages that have not been
confirmed delivered, persisted through an `IStorage` (`createLocalStorage` is
provided). The API is `addMessage(channel, msg)`, `getChannelMessages(channel)`,
and `clearChannel(channel)`; messages need an `id` and are deduped by it. The
usual wiring is `useSocketSendFailed` / `useSocketInFlightDrop` to enqueue and
`useSocketReady` to replay and clear on reconnect.

## Testing

`@luciodale/react-socket/testing` exposes `createMockTransport` / `MockTransport`
so tests drive the socket deterministically — open it, push a server frame, drop
the connection — without a real server or timers.

## Inspector

```tsx
import { InspectorPanel } from "@luciodale/react-socket/inspector"

<InspectorPanel manager={manager} />
```

Live traffic, subscription ref counts, in-flight entries, connection timeline.

## How it compares

**vs `react-use-websocket`** — that library is a thin hook around one socket:
`sendMessage` + `lastMessage`, and you hand-write routing, dedupe, and
restore-on-reconnect. react-socket types the protocol end to end and moves the
lifecycle into the library. https://koolcodez.com/projects/react-socket/docs/vs-react-use-websocket

**vs Socket.IO** — Socket.IO ships its own wire protocol and requires a Socket.IO
server; it also bundles rooms, namespaces, and HTTP long-poll fallback.
react-socket is plain WebSocket, client-only, and much smaller — you keep your
protocol and your server.
https://koolcodez.com/projects/react-socket/docs/vs-socket-io

## Typical use cases

Streaming LLM and agent clients, realtime trading and market-data UIs, chat,
collaborative editing, presence, live dashboards, and multiplayer demos.
